# Backup {visibility="uncounted"}

## What this does not do yet {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.callout-important}
Nobody outside the author team has built a model with this.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**In the proof of concept**

- The component library stops at basic epidemiological patterns. No
  partial pooling, and no mapping between latent and observed states
- Changing a component's order does not update the priors that go with
  it. That stays manual
- The abstraction layers have a runtime cost. We have not measured it
  properly
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
**In the claim**

- The design considerations came from the authors and have had no
  community input

::: {.callout-note}
`EpiAwareR`, Sebastian Funk's prototype R interface, ran two of the
three replications. That is the closest thing to outside use so far.
:::
:::
::::

## Reusing that AR(2) for South Korea {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The first replication takes the AR(2) from the worked example, a
  renewal process with a discretised serial interval, and a negative
  binomial observation model
- **A** to **C** are prior predictive checks on each part, **D**
  compares the continuous serial interval with its discretised form
- **E** and **F** recover the paper's finding. $R_t$ in South Korea
  peaked near 10 and dropped below 1 in early March 2020

::: {.attribution}
Replicating [Mishra et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16487).
Figure from the paper
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/composable-mishra.png){width="88%" fig-align="center"
fig-alt="Six panels: prior checks on each part, then the joint fit"}
:::
::::

## Swap the infection process, keep the rest {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- The third replication drops the renewal process and uses an SIR model
  built with `ODEProcess` over the SciML solvers instead
- Everything downstream is unchanged. A Poisson observation model, and
  a second version wrapping it in `Ascertainment` driven by an AR(1)
- **C** shows both landing on the same posterior $R_0$. **E** and **F**
  show the deterministic fit is the worse calibrated of the two

::: {.attribution}
Replicating Chatzilena et al. (2019),
[doi:10.1016/j.epidem.2019.100367][chatzilena]. An influenza outbreak
in an English boarding school, 1978. Figure 5 of the paper.
The paper's text reads $R_0 \approx 2$ off this panel. Panel C looks
closer to 4 to me, and I have not resolved which is right
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/composable-sir.png){width="88%" fig-align="center"
fig-alt="Six panels comparing a deterministic and a stochastic SIR fit"}
:::
::::

## Other ways to compose models {visibility="uncounted"}

+------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Approach                     | How it composes                     |
+==============================+=====================================+
| AlgebraicJulia               | Formal compositional guarantees,    |
|                              | and little support for              |
|                              | probabilistic models                |
+------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| `JuliaBUGS.jl`, `RxInfer.jl` | Models specified as graphs          |
+------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| `ModelingToolkit.jl`         | Acausal components, symbolically    |
+------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| `Gen.jl`                     | Nested generative functions, at a   |
|                              | lower level than `Turing.jl`        |
+------------------------------+-------------------------------------+

::: {.attribution}
The paper's discussion of alternative designs
:::

## LLM-assisted model construction {visibility="uncounted"}

- The component structure is what makes this tractable for a language
  model to assemble

::: {.attribution}
This claim is in the paper's discussion. It has not been tested.
:::

## The gap: COVID-19 showed what is possible {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- COVID-19 models integrated cases, prevalence, severity, and hospital
  occupancy for policy
- Fitting all the data and processes together provided evidence that
  supported policy decisions
- They required expertise across multiple domains and long development
  timelines

::: {.attribution}
Birrell et al. (2025),
[doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf030](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf030)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/composable-birrell.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Results from the England COVID-19 joint model"}
:::
::::

## The gap: flexibility for new contexts {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- In 2022 mpox spread internationally through sexual contact networks,
  and the response needed modelling quickly
- The COVID-19 models were not adapted to it. New single-source models
  were built instead
- A different contact structure and different behaviour needed explicit
  representation

::: {.attribution}
Endo et al. (2022),
[doi:10.1126/science.add4507](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add4507)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/composable-endo.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Results from the 2022 mpox sexual contact network model"}
:::
::::

## The gap: integrating diverse data {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Cross-sectional viral loads carry information about epidemic dynamics
- They are not in most policy models, even where they are already
  collected
- Adding a data source to an existing model means rebuilding it

::: {.attribution}
Hay et al. (2021),
[doi:10.1126/science.abh0635](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abh0635)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/composable-hay.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Title of the Hay et al. 2021 viral load paper"}
:::
::::

## The gap: multi-model efforts {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Multi-model efforts combine forecasts from several teams, and can
  improve predictive accuracy
- The teams rarely collaborate on model components
- Common components would let a difference in results be attributed to
  an assumption rather than an implementation

::: {.attribution}
The US COVID-19 Forecast Hub dataset. Cramer et al. (2022),
[doi:10.1038/s41597-022-01517-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01517-w)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/composable-cramer.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Title of the Cramer et al. 2022 Forecast Hub dataset paper"}
:::
::::
